questions.q: What did Joseph tell his steward to do with the brothers’ sacks before they left?
questions.a: Joseph told his steward to fill the brothers’ sacks with food, to put their money in the sacks, and to put his silver cup in the sack of the youngest one.

questions.q: Basically, what did Joseph tell the steward to say to the brothers when he overtook them outside the city?
questions.a: Joseph told the steward to ask them why they had returned evil for good and to accuse them of stealing Joseph’s cup.

questions.q: What did the brothers swear they would do if any one of them had stolen Joseph’s cup?
questions.a: The brothers said the one found with the cup would die, and the others would become slaves.

questions.q: What punishment did the steward say he would require if the stolen cup was found?
questions.a: The steward said that the one with whom the cup was found would be his slave, and the others would be innocent.

questions.q: What did the steward find and how did the brothers react?
questions.a: The steward found the cup in Benjamin’s sack; the brothers tore their clothes.

questions.q: What did the brothers do when they came back to Joseph in his house?
questions.a: The brothers bowed to the ground before Joseph.

questions.q: Who did Judah say had found out the sin of the brothers?
questions.a: Judah said that God had found out their sin.

questions.q: What did Judah say all the brothers would now become?
questions.a: Judah said all the brothers would now become Joseph’s slaves.

questions.q: What punishment did Joseph say he would require of the brothers?
questions.a: Joseph said that the man in whose hand the cup was found would be his slave and the rest could go in peace.

questions.q: What reasons did Judah give for why his father loved the youngest brother?
questions.a: Judah said that the youngest brother was the child of his father’s old age, and the only child left of his mother.

questions.q: What did the brothers worry would happen to their father if the youngest left him?
questions.a: The brothers worried their father would die if the youngest left him.

questions.q: Why did Judah say the brothers were forced to bring Benjamin with them to Egypt?
questions.a: Judah said they were forced to bring Benjamin because Joseph had said that unless the youngest brother comes, they would not see Joseph’s face.

questions.q: Why did Judah tell his father the brothers were forced to bring Benjamin with them to Egypt?
questions.a: Judah told his father that they were forced to bring Benjamin because Joseph had said that unless the youngest brother came, they would not see Joseph’s face.

questions.q: What did Israel think had happened to Joseph?
questions.a: Israel thought that surely Joseph had been torn in pieces.

questions.q: What did Israel say would happen to him if Benjamin were taken from him?
questions.a: Israel said that the brothers would bring down his gray hair with sorrow to Sheol.

questions.q: What did Judah say would happen to his father if they returned without Benjamin?
questions.a: Judah said that his father would die.

questions.q: What guarantee for Benjamin did Judah say he had become?
questions.a: Judah said that if he did not return Benjamin to his father, he would bear the guilt forever.

questions.q: What did Judah ask Joseph to do so that Benjamin could return to his father?
questions.a: Judah asked Joseph to make him Joseph’s slave, so that Benjamin could return to his father.

commentary.text: Joseph's policy to stay his brethren, and try their affection for Benjamin.

Verses 1–17 Joseph tried how his brethren felt towards Benjamin. Had they envied and hated the other son of Rachel as they had hated him, and if they had the same want of feeling towards their father Jacob as heretofore, they would now have shown it. When the cup was found upon Benjamin, they would have a pretext for leaving him to be a slave. But we cannot judge what men are now, by what they have been formerly; nor what they will do, by what they have done. The steward charged them with being ungrateful, rewarding evil for good; with folly, in taking away the cup of daily use, which would soon be missed, and diligent search made for it; for so it may be read, Is not this it in which my lord drinketh, as having a particular fondness for it, and for which he would search thoroughly? Or, By which, leaving it carelessly at your table, he would make trial whether you were honest men or not? They throw themselves upon Joseph's mercy, and acknowledge the righteousness of God, perhaps thinking of the injury they had formerly done to Joseph, for which they thought God was now reckoning with them. Even in afflictions wherein we believe ourselves wronged by men, we must own that God is righteous, and finds out our sin.

Had Joseph been, as Judah supposed him, an utter stranger to the family, he could not but be wrought upon by his powerful reasonings. But neither Jacob nor Benjamin need an intercessor with Joseph; for he himself loved them. Judah's faithful cleaving to Benjamin, now, in his distress, was recompensed long afterwards by the tribe of Benjamin keeping with the tribe of Judah, when the other tribes deserted it. The apostle, when discoursing of the mediation of Christ, observes, that our Lord sprang out of Judah, Heb 7:14; and he not only made intercession for the transgressors, but he became a Surety for them, testifying therein tender concern, both for his Father and for his brethren. Jesus, the great antitype of Joseph, humbles and proves his people, even after they have had some tastes of his loving-kindness. He brings their sins to their remembrance, that they may exercise and show repentance, and feel how much they owe to his mercy.
